timeoutPrompts: Masie: {PlayerName}? Please stay with me... the cellar pipes sound like they're groaning.
Masie: Hello? Did the damp brick wall swallow your voice?!
Masie: Talk to me... it's pitch black near the boiler and my hands are numb.
Masie: The line dropped... I have to try and muscle this valve alone.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*loud hiss of steam, water dripping somewhere deeper in the cellar* {PlayerName}? Oh, thank God. You're there.

Okay, I need you to talk to me for a second because I can barely hear myself think down here. The auxiliary line tripped, the heating riser is dropping fast, and the sensor in the tropical wing is already reading 52°F. If I can't get the bypass open soon, I'm going to lose a lot of the plants we've been growing for months.

I'm at the old cast-iron junction now. It's dark, it's wet, and I have absolutely no idea why I thought I could handle this by myself tonight. Can you stay on the line with me while I figure this out?

choices.choiceText: Breathe, Masie. I'm right here with you. What does the valve head look like?
Don't force it dry. Feel along the pipe collar for the mineral bleed screw.
Close your eyes for three seconds. Hear my voice through the noise. You've got this.
What tools do you have in your hands right now?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I've got the big brass pipe wrench, my old flashlight, and these garden gloves that are basically useless because everything down here is wet.

The floor is slick from the condensation, too. I nearly went down getting to the valve. I know I'm supposed to be calm about this because I've dealt with the boiler before, but right now I'm mostly annoyed that I'm scared.

Tell me what you want me to check first. I'm listening.

choices.choiceText: Drop the gloves. You need direct tactile grip on that wrench.
Check the pipe collar first for the mineral bleed screw.
Take the flashlight out of your teeth, set it on the dry brick ledge, and aim it at the valve.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
It's one of the old four-bolt gate valves. The yellow paint is still underneath all this buildup, but you can barely see it. There's green corrosion around the metal and white mineral crust everywhere.

I've tried turning the wheel by hand twice. Nothing. My hands are slipping and I don't want to put so much force into it that I make something worse. Give me a second... okay. I'm looking at it properly now.

What are you seeing that I'm missing?

choices.choiceText: Take the gloves off. Grip the iron directly with a dry shop rag.
Seat the jaws of your pipe wrench across two spokes of the wheel.
Look around for a copper hammer or a heavy spanner to tap the housing.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Wait. I found something. There's a little square brass screw on the elbow joint. It's almost completely buried under the corrosion.

I'm nervous about touching it. It looks like the kind of thing that hasn't moved since before I was born, and I really don't want to find out what's sitting behind it the hard way.

Do you think I should ease it loose, or leave it alone and work on the main wheel?

choices.choiceText: Only a tiny hiss of vapor. Back it off half a turn to release the vacuum lock.
Keep your face turned away, wrap your sleeve around the wrench, and crack it gently.
Don't touch the screw if you feel unsafe—focus directly on the main wheel instead.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*sharp inhale, then a slower breath out* Okay. I'm doing it.

You'd laugh if you could see me. Twenty minutes ago I was arguing with a professor about greenhouse humidity like it was the most important thing in the world. Now I'm sitting in a freezing cellar with a flashlight and a wrench, trying not to panic.

But your voice is helping. I can actually focus again. I'm looking at the wheel now. It's completely locked with mineral buildup.

choices.choiceText: Good girl. Use your pipe wrench handle to tap the casing and crack that crust.
Wrap a cloth around the rim and get ready to pull.
Check the counterweight arm above the manifold before we apply torque.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I see it. There's a counterweight arm sitting above the manifold, and it's pressed right against the safety stop.

I don't remember ever seeing it this tightly seated. I could probably move it, but I don't want to guess with a boiler. That's how people get hurt, and I've had enough close calls for one night already.

What would you do from where I'm standing?

choices.choiceText: No, it vents outside through the copper roof flues. Lift the arm two inches!
Keep the counterweight down and focus purely on the bypass wheel.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Okay... I'm lifting it. Slowly.

*mechanical clack, then a sudden rush of air* Oh. Wow. Okay. That dropped the pressure.

Hang on. The wheel moved. Not much, but it moved. That's the first sign all night that this thing is actually going to cooperate with me.

I'm going back to the valve. My hands are shaking a little, but at least they're shaking because I can feel this working now.

choices.choiceText: Now seat the wrench across the spokes and pull!
Turn the wheel counter-clockwise until the needle hits 20 PSI!

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I wrapped the rag around the rim. Better grip.

My boots are planted, my gloves are off, and I'm trying to stop relying on my arms alone. The metal is freezing. I can feel the edge of the wheel pressing into my palms.

I don't love this. But okay. I'm ready. Count me in.

choices.choiceText: Put your shoulder into it. Pull toward your chest on three. One... two... three!
Drop your center of gravity. Use your legs to lever the turn, not just your arms.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I've got the wrench across the spokes. It's wedged in pretty well.

I had to adjust my footing because the floor is still wet, but I think I've got enough leverage now. Give me one second... yeah. I can feel the whole valve resisting me.

All right. I'm going to pull. Don't let me overthink it.

choices.choiceText: Heave down on it, Masie! Don't let it slip!
Lean your whole weight on the handle—snap the mineral lock!

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*hiss of air, then a quick splash against metal* Okay—there it is. Just a little burst, but enough to make me jump.

My wrist got a bit of warm mist on it. Nothing serious. The pressure definitely changed, though. I can feel the spindle move now, just slightly.

That was the first thing down here that actually sounded normal. I'm going for the wheel while it's loose.

choices.choiceText: Now grab the wheel! Turn it counter-clockwise while the seal is warm!
Lock the wrench on the spokes and finish the turn!

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*sharp metallic taps echo off the brick* That's doing something. Pieces of the buildup are breaking loose now.

There are flakes all over my boots, and I can finally see more of the threads underneath. I honestly can't believe how badly this thing was seized up.

Okay. The wheel looks better. I'm going to set the wrench again and try it before it decides to lock up on me a second time.

choices.choiceText: Now lock the wrench in place and lean your body weight down!
Wrap the cloth around the rim and pull with both hands!

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*grunt of effort, followed by a long scrape of metal* Oh—there. It moved.

It actually moved.

*deep thud through the pipes, followed by the boiler catching* Wait. That's the burner. It's on.

The whole jacket is vibrating now. I can hear the water starting to move through the line. I'm not celebrating yet because I don't want to jinx it, but... I think we got it.

choices.choiceText: Spin it four more rotations until the riser pipe sings!
Step back from the valve! Watch the steam gauge on the main tank!
Listen for any pressure leaks along the seams before you let go.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I'm checking the flanges now.

Nothing obvious. No sharp hissing, no steam shooting out anywhere it shouldn't. Just that steady mechanical sound from the water moving through the system.

I can finally hear myself breathe. Give me a second to make sure I'm not missing something stupid because I'm still running on adrenaline.

choices.choiceText: Look at the gauge needle. What is it reading?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
The gauge is climbing. Eighteen... twenty... twenty-two.

That's it. That's the pressure we needed.

I can already feel the heat coming back through the overhead lines. The pipes are warming up, and the air isn't biting anymore. I don't think I've been this relieved over a piece of machinery in my entire life.

Let me check the greenhouse. I need to see the seedlings with my own eyes.

choices.choiceText: You did it, Masie. The seedlings are safe. Every single one of them.
Listen to that boiler hum. You're an absolute force of nature.
Step away from the heat riser. Let the cast iron do the work now.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*slides down against the brick wall, breathing hard* Oh my God.

Give me a second. My legs are actually shaking.

I know how dramatic that sounds, but I really thought I'd have to watch all of that work die because I couldn't get one stupid valve open. Those plants aren't just plants to me. I've spent months on them. Late nights, failed samples, grant money, arguing with people who think I'm overprotective of a bunch of leaves.

And you stayed here the whole time. I don't think you realize how much that mattered.

choices.choiceText: You kept your own head straight, Masie. I was just holding the line.
How do your hands feel? Did you scrape yourself on the iron?
Take as long as you need on that step. Just breathe the warm air.
I'm so proud of you. That was terrifying and you didn't back down.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Don't do that. Don't make it smaller than it was.

Being alone down here made everything feel ten times worse. I kept thinking, 'Just handle it. You've fixed things before. Don't be ridiculous.' But after a while that just turns into silence, and silence gets inside your head.

Hearing you on the other end gave me something else to focus on. It felt like there was a person in the room with me, even though there wasn't.

choices.choiceText: You'll never have to face a cold cellar alone again.
It was never empty as long as you had the courage to pick up that wrench.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
My palms are filthy, and I scraped my thumb on the flange. It's nothing serious. Just enough to sting when the adrenaline wears off.

Actually... my hands feel warm again now. I didn't notice how cold they were until a minute ago.

You know, you're very good at asking the practical questions when I'm too distracted to ask them myself. I appreciate that more than I probably sound like I do.

choices.choiceText: That's the best smell in the world when it means life survived.
Wash that scrape under clean water as soon as we head upstairs.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*slow breath, then a quiet laugh* Okay. The heat is finally getting to me.

It's strange how quickly your body catches up once it realizes the emergency is over. My shoulders were practically up around my ears.

I think I was holding my breath this whole time. I can finally feel myself coming back down to earth.

choices.choiceText: Come on up out of the dark. Let's see the glasshouse now that it's safe.
Stay on the step for another minute if your legs still feel like jelly.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*voice goes quieter for a moment* Nobody's said that to me in a long time.

The department mostly notices when something breaks. My family notices when I'm not following the life they imagined for me. Most of the time, I just hear what still needs to be done.

So... thank you. Seriously. I know it's just a sentence, but I needed to hear it more than I realized.

choices.choiceText: Because I see how much devotion you pour into this place. Come up to the light.
Your parents don't understand what it means to keep a living ecosystem alive.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
You know what's embarrassing? I've spent years being very proud of the fact that I never need anyone.

I carry things myself. I fix things myself. I stay late and tell people I'm fine even when I'm exhausted. It's useful until you realize you've turned being alone into part of your identity.

Sitting here with you on the line tonight made me notice how tired I am of doing that. Not helpless. Just... tired.

choices.choiceText: Armor is heavy to carry every day. It's okay to set it down.
Self-reliance is admirable, but sharing the load makes life softer.
You don't have to carry the whole conservatory on your own shoulders anymore.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*boots on the steps, then the greenhouse door opening* Come on. I'm going back upstairs.

Oh... yeah. You need to hear this.

The misting system just kicked on. Everything is damp again, the glass is fogging up, and the whole place looks completely different now that the heat is back. Five minutes ago I thought this room was going to be a disaster. Now it just feels quiet.

I'm walking toward the main house. Stay with me.

choices.choiceText: Describe it to me. What does it look like through your eyes?
Walk over to the water lily pond. Let's sit where it's peaceful.
Check the seedling trays on the bench first. Are the leaves upright?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I'm at the potting bench.

Okay... they're upright.

The leaves are wet with condensation, but they're still firm. No obvious damage around the edges. The trays held their heat better than I expected.

I know they probably look like ordinary plants to anyone else. Right now, though? Seeing them still standing is making me want to sit down again.

choices.choiceText: That's a miracle of timing. Now take a seat by the pond.
Describe the glasshouse to me right now. Paint the picture.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
The glass is covered in condensation, so the lights outside are all blurred. Everything beyond the panes looks farther away than it really is.

The tree ferns are catching the mist, the floor is wet, and the copper pipes overhead are finally warming up again. It doesn't look magical or anything. It just looks like a place that's alive and finally settled down.

After what happened downstairs, honestly, that's enough for me.

choices.choiceText: A sunken airship with you... I'd happily stay underwater forever.
It sounds like a forgotten world that only you know how to wake up.
How does the air feel against your skin after that freezing cellar?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
It's warm in here now. Humid, a little heavy, and it smells like wet soil and old wood.

There are still traces of the boiler smell on my clothes. I probably smell terrible.

But the air feels good. The kind of good where you notice your body unclenching without realizing it was tense in the first place.

choices.choiceText: Take me to your bench by the pond. Let's just sit in that blanket.
It sounds like a place where time completely stops moving.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*small laugh* You really do know how to make me smile when I'm trying to stay serious.

But... yeah. It does feel separate from everything tonight. My phone usually means emails, deadlines, somebody asking where a report is. Right now it just means you're still there.

I could get used to that.

choices.choiceText: Take me to your bench by the pond. I want to know what you think about when it's this quiet.
The city can stay outside. We're safe in here.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
That's basically why I'm in this field.

People joke that I spend my life taking care of plants, but there's so much history in here. Every species has a reason it's here. Every little system we've built is trying to keep something alive long enough for us to understand it.

I think that's what I care about more than anything. Taking something fragile seriously.

choices.choiceText: And tonight you kept that negotiation alive. Let's head to the water lilies.
You speak about plants with the reverence most people reserve for art.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Exactly.

That's the part I wish people understood. Plants aren't decorative background. Some of them have been adapting for longer than any human story we tell ourselves.

You look at an old species and realize you're looking at something that survived conditions we'll never experience. It puts my own problems in perspective without making them disappear.

choices.choiceText: That perspective makes daily human worries feel so small.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*soft footsteps over wet slate, water moving nearby* I'm by the pond now.

This is usually where I come when I don't want to be around anyone. It's quiet enough that you can hear the fountain instead of your own thoughts.

I'm sitting on the edge. The stone's warm from the pipes underneath. For the first time tonight, I'm not listening for something going wrong.

choices.choiceText: Is your little resident bullfrog out tonight?
Dip your fingers in the water. Let the rest of the day wash off.
What does the sky look like through the curved glass right now?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
It's dark blue outside. There's a light drizzle, and the drops are running down the glass in little lines.

The campus lights are on in the distance, but they're soft through the fog. It's actually really nice.

I spend so much time in here working that I forget to stop and look up. Tonight I finally have a reason to.

choices.choiceText: Is the resident bullfrog keeping you company in your cathedral?
Dip your hands in the pool. Let the soot wash away.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*soft splash* He's still here.

He's sitting on the little terracotta saucer like he owns the place. He looked at me when I walked over, then made that ridiculous low croak he does.

I swear he only respects me when I have food. Which is fair. I haven't exactly been a model host lately.

choices.choiceText: Tell him he owes us rent assistance next month.
He knows he has the best guardian on campus.
Does he have an official name, or is he just 'The Bullfrog'?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
His name is Barnaby.

He turned up after a storm a few years ago and never really left. I started keeping notes on him for fun, then it became an actual part of my research because I apparently don't know how to leave anything alone.

He spends most of the day hiding under the plants. At night he comes out and acts like he pays tuition here.

choices.choiceText: Barnaby has excellent taste in sanctuaries.
Tell Barnaby that on Saturday, he's sharing his pond with me.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*quiet ripple of water* I'm putting my fingers in.

It's warmer than I expected.

There's still dirt and grease on my hands, and it's all washing off slowly. I know that's a very small thing, but right now it feels good to do something that doesn't require me to solve anything.

choices.choiceText: You fought hard tonight. You deserve every second of this peace.
Lean back against the stone rim. Let the calm take over.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*laughs* Honestly, that's probably fair.

Barnaby's contribution to the greenhouse is mostly eating bugs and sitting in places he's not supposed to. He still somehow manages to look like the most qualified employee here.

He's been around long enough that I notice when he isn't in his usual spot.

choices.choiceText: Until I show up on Saturday to apply for the position.
He knows a dedicated guardian when he sees one.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Guardian is a nicer word than the ones I've heard from my family.

When I switched from pre-law to plant sciences, my father asked me what I planned to do with it. When I told him, he basically said I'd traded a real career for taking care of weeds.

I laughed at the time because I didn't want him to know it hurt. It did, though.

choices.choiceText: Your father couldn't see the cathedral you were building. His loss.
Weeds are just plants that don't need human permission to be strong.
Did that comment make you doubt yourself at the time?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
For a while, yeah.

I kept wondering whether I'd made some huge mistake and just didn't have the courage to admit it. I'd walk into the greenhouse and feel happy, then feel guilty for being happy because it wasn't the life they wanted for me.

It took me a long time to stop treating their disappointment like proof that I'd done something wrong.

choices.choiceText: It takes infinitely more courage. You built a sanctuary with your own hands.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*laughs softly* Barnaby would make you earn it.

He has standards. Apparently they involve sitting still, not making sudden movements, and keeping your snacks where he can see them.

But... I'd probably approve your application before he does.

choices.choiceText: What does your ideal Saturday afternoon look like with me?
I'll bring treats for Barnaby and fresh bread for you.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
He wanted something very different for me.

In his mind, success meant a good salary, a respectable title, an office where people could see what I'd accomplished. I understand where that came from. He wanted me to be secure.

I just don't think he understood that I feel more like myself here than I ever did trying to become the person he had in his head.

choices.choiceText: Because you measure wealth in things that grow, not things that decay.
True wealth is having peace in your chest when you go to sleep.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
That's what I like about them.

A weed doesn't care whether you think it belongs there. It finds a crack, gets enough light, and keeps going.

I think I needed that lesson when I was younger. I spent too much time waiting for somebody to tell me I was allowed to choose my own life.

choices.choiceText: You already have that resilience, Masie. You broke through the asphalt years ago.
Defiance doesn't have to be loud. Sometimes it's just surviving in quiet soil.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*quiet rustle of her sweater* I'm just sitting here with my knees up.

It's funny. An hour ago I was convinced the worst thing that could happen tonight was a dead boiler. Now I'm realizing the bigger thing was how completely alone I felt before you picked up.

This is probably the first time in a while I've sat somewhere without thinking about what I should be fixing next.

choices.choiceText: Because you aren't carrying the glasshouse alone anymore.
Safety is having someone who answers when the cold creeps in.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Maybe I was.

I used to tell myself that being alone was peaceful because nobody could disappoint me. That part was true.

I just never admitted the other side of it. Nobody could get close enough to know me either. Tonight feels like a pretty uncomfortable reason to realize that, but I'm glad I did.

choices.choiceText: You never have to hide with me, Masie. I'm right here.
Opening up takes strength, especially after being judged.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Can I tell you something?

I don't usually talk this much about myself. I tend to think people get bored when I go too far into things, so I keep it simple and change the subject.

But with you, I don't feel like I'm performing. I can say what I actually mean, even when it's not particularly flattering or well thought out.

That's rare for me.

choices.choiceText: Because when you care about someone, you listen to the roots, not just the leaves.
Maybe we were looking for the same quiet corner of the world all along.
It's easy to understand someone whose soul is as honest as yours.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*a quiet laugh that fades into a breath* That's... really nice.

Most people listen for the part where they can jump in. They don't really listen for what somebody is trying not to say.

And I know we've only been talking for a while, but tonight I don't feel like I have to explain every little piece of myself before you'll understand what I'm getting at.

choices.choiceText: You are safe with me, Masie. On every level.
Tell me about Saturday. Walk me through our afternoon together.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
Maybe that's what this is.

Not some huge, dramatic thing. Just finding someone who likes the same kind of quiet.

I always thought being understood would feel bigger than this. Turns out it's actually pretty simple. It's just not having to edit yourself every thirty seconds.

choices.choiceText: Tell me about Saturday. Walk me through our afternoon.
A rare hybrid in the snow... that's exactly what you are.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
All right. Saturday.

Come through the little iron gate behind the botany hall around two. I'll leave it unlatched.

I'll probably be in the greenhouse already, pretending I wasn't checking the clock every five minutes. We can repot my grandmother's cactus, make tea, and sit by the pond afterward. Nothing fancy.

Honestly, I'd rather have a normal afternoon with you than some big date where we're both trying to impress each other.

choices.choiceText: And what about the tea you promised me?
I'm going to hold your hands while we set the roots.
Tell me more about your grandmother's cactus before we pot it.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
My grandmother got it from her mother in the eighties. It was just one little cutting back then.

It survived a lot. Moves, bad windows, years when nobody knew what they were doing, the whole thing.

When my grandmother got sick, I was more worried about that cactus than I was about most of the things people thought were valuable in her house. When she died, everyone else was picking jewelry. I took the pot.

It sounds sentimental, I know. I just like having one thing that kept going with us.

choices.choiceText: She'd be so proud to know it's thriving in your hands.
Sharing a piece of that cactus with me... that's the greatest gift I could ever receive.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*soft laugh* Then you'll have to accept that you'll leave with dirt under your nails.

We'll take the cutting, get it set properly, and I'll probably tell you three times not to overwater it because I can't help myself.

But... yeah. I'd like that. Doing something quiet together instead of trying to fill every second with conversation.

choices.choiceText: And then we drink tea by the lilies.
I don't mind the soil as long as your hands are in mine.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I have spearmint and some dried verbena in the greenhouse kitchen.

We'll make two mugs, sit on the stone edge by the lilies, and let the day be over for a while. No work talk unless we actually want to talk about it.

No notifications, no deadlines, no pretending we're having the perfect date. Just tea and whatever comes up.

That sounds pretty good to me right now.

choices.choiceText: That sounds like heaven on earth, Masie.
I'll bring warm sourdough bread from the bakery down my street to share.
What if it rains on Saturday afternoon?

nodes.partnerDialogue:
If it rains, we stay inside.

Honestly, I'd prefer that. Rain on the glass makes the whole place quieter. We can sit by the pond and listen to it while the greenhouse stays warm.

And if you bring that sourdough you keep threatening me with, I'm going to have a hard time pretending I'm not impressed.

choices.choiceText: Then I'm crossing my fingers for rain.
I'll definitely bring that warm sourdough bread.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*laughs* Okay, now you're making this very difficult for me.

Fresh sourdough, salted butter, tea, Barnaby pretending he's in charge... that's dangerously close to my idea of an actual date.

I like that it's simple. I don't need anything elaborate. I'd rather remember a good conversation than an expensive dinner.

choices.choiceText: I wouldn't complain for a single second.
Barnaby and I will take turns patrolling the lily pads.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
*long, steady breath* The boiler sounds normal now.

The greenhouse is back around 70°F, the seedlings are fine, and I can finally feel how tired I am.

Thank you for answering tonight. Really.

And thank you for talking to me like I was a person who needed help, not a problem you had to solve. I don't think you realize how different that felt.

choices.choiceText: I'll always pick up when you call, Masie. Always.
Go get some rest on that dorm mattress. You saved a whole world tonight.
Sleep gently, my greenhouse guardian.

nodes.partnerDialogue:
I'm going to pack up and head upstairs.

I'll leave the south gate key on my desk so I don't forget it for Saturday. I know I'm probably going to wake up tomorrow and wonder why I told you half the things I just told you.

But... I'm glad I did.

Go get some sleep, okay? And send me a message when you wake up so I know you made it through the night too.

Goodnight, {PlayerName}. See you Saturday.

choices.choiceText: [Hang Up and Return to Chat]
